subquery.def: A query inside another query, in brackets. The outer query uses its result as a value, a list, or a table.

scalar-subquery.def: A subquery that returns exactly one value, one row and one column, so it can stand wherever a single value can.

correlated-subquery.def: A subquery that uses a column of the outer query, so it's evaluated again for each outer row.

exists.def: True if the subquery returns at least one row. It stops at the first match; NOT EXISTS finds rows with no match.

derived-table.def: A subquery in FROM, used as if it were a table. It needs an alias.

cte.def: Common table expression: a named subquery written first, with WITH. Later steps read it like a table, top to bottom.

recursive-cte.def: A CTE that refers to itself: a starting row, a step that builds the next rows, and a condition that stops it. Used for dates, trees and paths.

lines.hook.1: Some questions need the answer to another question first.
lines.hook.2: Which products cost more than average? First, you need the average.
lines.hook.3: SQL lets you put a query inside a query. That's this lesson.
lines.scalar.1: Here are the eight products and their prices.

scalar.2.caption: The inner query, in brackets, runs first. It works out one number: the average price, 4.51.
scalar.2.voice: The inner query, in brackets, runs first. It works out one number: the average price, four fifty-one.

lines.scalar.3: The outer query then compares every price with that number. Four products beat it.
lines.scalar.4: A query inside a query is a <k>subquery</k>. One that returns a single value is a <k id="scalar-subquery">scalar subquery</k>.
lines.scalar.5: It must return exactly one value. Two rows, and PostgreSQL stops with an error.
lines.later.1: Your turn. Which customers joined after Lena?
lines.later.ask: Compare each join date with Lena's, found by a subquery.

later.hint.caption: WHERE joined > (SELECT joined FROM customers WHERE name = 'Lena')
later.hint.voice: Where joined is later than the result of: select joined from customers where the name is Lena.

lines.later.error: The database couldn't run that. Check the brackets around the subquery.
lines.later.extra: Too many customers. Is Lena's own date in the comparison?
lines.later.missing: Some customers are missing. Later means greater than.
lines.later.done: Six customers joined after Lena. The subquery found her date, so you didn't have to.
lines.list.1: A subquery can also return a list. Which customers bought a cake?
lines.list.2: The inner query finds the customer IDs on cake orders. Customer seven shows up twice.
lines.list.3: IN checks each customer against that list. Ana, Raj, Yuki and Ines. Duplicates in the list don't matter.
lines.corr.1: Harder question: which products cost more than the average of their own category?
lines.corr.2: Now the inner query uses the outer row's category. For bread it averages the breads, for cake the cakes.
lines.corr.3: It runs again for every product. That's a <k id="correlated-subquery">correlated subquery</k>.
lines.corr.ask: How many products beat their own category's average?
lines.corr.two: More than that. Every category has a winner, and bread has two.
lines.corr.four: Four. One or two from each category.
lines.corr.six: Fewer. Only the top of each category clears its own average. It's four.
lines.corr.4: Sourdough and rye beat the bread average, cinnamon roll beats the pastries, and lemon tart beats the cakes.
lines.exists.1: Which customers have at least one pending order?
lines.exists.2: <k>EXISTS</k> asks: is there any row? It stops at the first match, and ignores what the subquery selects.
lines.exists.3: Maya and Omar. And NOT EXISTS finds customers with no such row: the anti-join from the joins lesson, spelled out.
lines.never.1: Your turn. Find customers who have no paid orders at all.
lines.never.ask: Use NOT EXISTS with a subquery on orders.

never.hint.caption: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid')
never.hint.voice: Where not exists: select one from orders, where the order's customer is this customer, and the status is paid.

lines.never.error: The database couldn't run that. Read the message under the editor.
lines.never.extra: Too many customers. Does the subquery match on this customer's ID?
lines.never.missing: Someone's missing. Customers with no orders at all have no paid orders either.
lines.never.done: Lena, Theo, and Raj, whose only order was refunded.
lines.cte.1: Last idea. What's the average number of orders per customer, and who's above it?
lines.cte.2: That's two steps: count each customer's orders, then compare with the average count. Nested, it gets hard to read.
lines.cte.3: WITH names the first step, counts. The next step reads it like a table. That's a <k id="cte">CTE</k>.

cte.4.caption: The average is 1.75. Maya, Omar, Ana and Yuki are above it.
cte.4.voice: The average is one point seven five. Maya, Omar, Ana and Yuki are above it.

lines.cte.5: A subquery in FROM does the same job. It's called a <k id="derived-table">derived table</k>. CTEs just read top to bottom.
lines.cte.6: One more kind: a <k id="recursive-cte">recursive CTE</k> builds rows step by step, like a list of dates. Explore has one to try.
lines.above.1: Your turn. Write the whole query: customers with more orders than the average customer.
lines.above.ask: Finish the query below the CTE.

above.hint.caption: Join counts to customers, and keep n > (SELECT AVG(n) FROM counts).
above.hint.voice: Join counts to customers, and keep the rows where n is more than the average n from counts.

lines.above.error: The database couldn't run that. The message under the editor says where.
lines.above.extra: Too many rows. Compare each count with the average.
lines.above.missing: Some customers are missing. Greater than the average, not equal to the maximum.
lines.above.columns: Two columns: the name, and the count.
lines.above.done: Maya, Omar, Ana and Yuki. Two named steps, read top to bottom.

quiz.q1.caption: WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products). What must the subquery return?
quiz.q1.voice: Where price is more than a subquery that averages the prices. What must that subquery return?
quiz.q1.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q1-why: It's compared with one price, so it must be one value: one row, one column.
lines.quiz.q2-why: It uses a column from the outer query, so its result depends on the outer row.

quiz.q3.caption: Why do people write EXISTS (SELECT 1 …)?
quiz.q3.voice: Why do people write exists, select one?
quiz.q3.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q3-why: EXISTS only asks whether a row exists. What the subquery selects is ignored, so one is a convention.

quiz.q4.caption: Why use a CTE instead of nesting subqueries?
quiz.q4.speaker: interviewer

lines.quiz.q4-why: It names each step, so the query reads top to bottom, and a step can be used more than once.

quiz.retry.caption: {right} / 4. Worth another pass.
quiz.retry.voice: Not quite there. Replay a chapter or two, then try again.

lines.keywords.1: Before we wrap up, here are the words worth keeping.
lines.keywords.ask: Flip each card. Star the ones you want to practise later.
lines.keywords.hint: Tap a card to flip it. Press Done when you're ready.
lines.keywords.done: Starred words go to your flashcards. A few minutes a day keeps them fresh.
lines.finish.1: That's the lesson. Subqueries answer the question behind the question. Correlated ones run per row. And CTEs name the steps.
lines.finish.2: Next up: keeping every row, with window functions.
